challenges.name: Steady Mop
challenges.note: Held the floor mop the whole pass, first try

hazards.cross-wipe-cloth: That's the cloth you just used on the toilet, sitting on the sink edge like it's clean. Working dirty to clean instead of clean to dirty puts what came off the toilet onto the next surface a hand actually touches.
hazards.gloves-only-box: That box is exam gloves, and nothing else is on over your uniform yet. Contact precautions are a barrier, not a glove — gloves go on last, over a gown's cuffs, not as the whole outfit.
hazards.regular-trash-bin: That bin is unlined general trash, and the wipe in your hand came off a visibly soiled surface. Regulated waste goes in the red bag by the door, not into a bin that ends up in the same truck as the break-room trash.
hazards.shaken-linen: That sheet is mid-shake. Snapping soiled linen out before it goes in the bag is exactly how whatever is on it gets airborne and lands on a surface you already disinfected — bag it where it lies, don't shake it first.

interrupts.alert: While rolling the linen, something hard and small drops out of the folds onto the floor — it looks like a used syringe cap.
interrupts.cue: That is not yours to pick up or dispose of.
interrupts.missNote: The linen bag went to laundry with an unresolved sharp on the floor beside it. Whoever mops that spot next has no idea it's there.
interrupts.why: A sharp that turns up somewhere it shouldn't be is a nursing call every time, not a judgment call for whoever happens to be holding the linen — the room stays as it is around that spot until someone qualified to handle it does.
interrupts.wrongNote: It's the phone to nursing — a sharp in the wrong place gets reported before the turnover continues around it.

interrupts.alert: A supply cart passing in the hallway clips the wet floor sign and knocks it flat, right as you're finishing the pass.
interrupts.cue: The floor is still wet and the doorway now has no sign standing at it.
interrupts.missNote: The sign stayed down through the rest of the pass. Anyone who walked through that doorway had no warning the floor inside was wet.
interrupts.why: A sign flat on the floor warns nobody — the doorway needs it standing again immediately, because the wet floor it's supposed to be warning people about hasn't gone anywhere just because the sign fell over.
interrupts.wrongNote: It's the sign — stand it back up at the doorway before anything else continues.

lateNotes.clean-log: Hold that. PPE comes off and the floor has to be dry before this room logs as ready.
lateNotes.wet-floor-sign: Not yet — the sign goes down before the mop does, not the other way around.

name: Isolation Room Turnover

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Check the card on the door for what kind of precautions this room is under.
steps.prompt: Check the card on the door for what kind of precautions this room is under.
steps.title: Read the posted precautions before entering
steps.why: The card on the door is what tells you which PPE this room actually needs — contact, droplet or both — before a single glove goes on. Guessing at it from the last room you cleaned is how the wrong barrier goes up on the wrong room.

steps.cue: Gown first, then gloves pulled up over the gown's cuffs, then eye protection.
steps.prompt: Gown first, then gloves pulled up over the gown's cuffs, then eye protection.
steps.title: Don PPE to the posted precautions
steps.why: The CDC's transmission-based precautions guidance orders PPE donning for a reason: a gown put on after gloves leaves a gap at the wrist that a glove alone was never meant to cover, and eye protection last means it's the one thing you're not tempted to touch again once your hands are already dirty.

steps.cue: Two things in this room are for nursing to deal with, not you. Find them before you touch anything else.

itemNames.overfull-sharps: a sharps container packed past its line
itemNames.stray-sharp: an uncapped needle on the bedside tray

itemNotes.overfull-sharps: An overfilled sharps container is a clinical device past a fill line, not a housekeeping item to empty or force closed. Flag it for nursing and keep moving.
itemNotes.stray-sharp: A loose needle on a bedside tray is not an EVS job — it goes untouched and nursing gets called, the same as the syringe cap you'll find in the linen in a minute.

steps.prompt: Two things in this room are for nursing to deal with, not you. Find them before you touch anything else.
steps.title: Scan the room for what isn't yours to handle
steps.why: An EVS tech's scope stops at the room, not at every object in it — a sharp or a device left behind by clinical staff gets flagged, not picked up, because handling it wrong is a needlestick this job was never trained for in the first place.

steps.cue: Roll the linen inward on itself and place it straight into the hamper bag.
steps.prompt: Roll the linen inward on itself and place it straight into the hamper bag.
steps.title: Bag the soiled linen without shaking it
steps.why: Soiled linen carries whatever the patient did, and CDC guidance is explicit that it gets handled with minimum agitation — rolled and bagged, never shaken, snapped or held against the body, because shaking it is how it gets into the air of a room you're trying to clean.

steps.cue: Put visibly soiled disposables in the red biohazard bag, not the general trash.
steps.prompt: Put visibly soiled disposables in the red biohazard bag, not the general trash.
steps.title: Sort regulated waste into the red bag
steps.why: OSHA's bloodborne pathogens standard treats anything soaked or caked with blood or other potentially infectious material as regulated waste with its own bag, its own hauler and its own disposal rule — mixing it into general trash turns every bag handler downstream into someone exposed without knowing it.

steps.cue: Wipe the high-touch surfaces and watch the panel — commit once the surface has stayed visibly wet long enough, per the label.

gauge.label: SURFACE WET TIME
gauge.missNote: Committed before the label's wet-contact time was met, or well after the surface had already dried — neither one is a disinfected surface.

steps.prompt: Wipe the high-touch surfaces and watch the panel — commit once the surface has stayed visibly wet long enough, per the label.
steps.title: Hold every high-touch surface to its wet-contact time
steps.why: A disinfectant only kills what its label says it kills for as long as the surface actually stays wet — that contact time is set by the product's own registered label, not by how fast the wipe feels done, and wiping it dry early means the surface was never actually disinfected at all.

steps.cue: Wipe the sink and counter, then the toilet — never the other way around.
steps.outOfOrderNote: Sink and counter before the toilet, every time — the order is what keeps the dirtiest surface from touching the cleanest one.
steps.prompt: Wipe the sink and counter, then the toilet — never the other way around.
steps.title: Clean the bathroom cleanest surface first
steps.why: Cleaning cleanest-to-dirtiest keeps whatever came off the toilet from ever reaching the counter a patient's hand or toothbrush touches next — reverse the order and the cloth becomes the thing that cross-contaminates the surface you already finished.

steps.cue: Fit a fresh liner in the trash and the red bag holder before moving on.
steps.prompt: Fit a fresh liner in the trash and the red bag holder before moving on.
steps.title: Reline the emptied bins
steps.why: A bin left unlined is a bin the next person in this room reaches for and finds nothing — relining it now is what makes the room actually ready, not just emptied.

steps.cue: Unhook the curtain and bag it for laundry rather than leaving it up.
steps.prompt: Unhook the curtain and bag it for laundry rather than leaving it up.
steps.title: Take down the soiled privacy curtain
steps.why: A privacy curtain gets touched by every hand that passes the bed, and CDC surface guidance treats it the same as any other high-touch item in a precautions room — left up, it carries the last patient's risk straight into the next one's stay.

steps.cue: Place the sign at the doorway before the mop touches the floor.

drag.missNote: Not at the doorway — the one place someone actually walks in from is the one place the sign has to stand.

steps.prompt: Place the sign at the doorway before the mop touches the floor.
steps.title: Set the wet floor sign before mopping
steps.why: A wet floor with no sign at the door is a fall waiting on whoever walks in next — the sign goes up before the mop, not after someone has already slipped on a floor they had no way to know was wet.

steps.cue: Work in overlapping strokes from the far corner back toward the door and hold the pass steady.
steps.holdBreakNote: The pass broke before it reached the door. A mop stroke that stops partway leaves a patch that never got cleaned, not a floor that's merely still drying.
steps.prompt: Work in overlapping strokes from the far corner back toward the door and hold the pass steady.
steps.title: Mop the floor working back to the door
steps.why: Mopping toward the door instead of away from it means you're never standing on floor you haven't cleaned yet, and never re-tracking dirty water back over a section you already finished.

steps.cue: Gloves off first, then hand hygiene, then the gown, then the mask or eye protection last.
steps.outOfOrderNote: Gloves, then hands washed, then the gown, then the mask last — that order is what keeps a contaminated glove away from your bare skin.
steps.prompt: Gloves off first, then hand hygiene, then the gown, then the mask or eye protection last.
steps.title: Doff PPE in the order that keeps you clean
steps.why: The CDC's doffing sequence exists because the most contaminated items come off first and the ones nearest your airway come off last, with a hand-hygiene step between them — skip the order and a hand that just peeled off a soiled glove is the hand about to touch your own face.

steps.cue: Mark the room terminally cleaned and release it to bed management.
steps.prompt: Mark the room terminally cleaned and release it to bed management.
steps.title: Log the room and release it
steps.why: Bed management assigns this room to its next patient off this log, not off a guess that the door being open means it's ready — an unlogged room is a room that either sits empty longer than it needs to or gets assigned before it's actually done.

supportLine: your employer's employee assistance program, or SEIU-UHW's member resources if a room like this one has you rattled
tagline: PPE donned to the posted precautions, linen bagged not shaken, regulated waste kept separate, every high-touch surface held to its label's wet-contact time, and the room logged clean and released
